description: Every great mission starts with a single line of code. Diverse crew of Students: to decode the universe’s most pressing problems. From local climate action to deep space exploration, we are building tools that matter.
summary:
Earth’s surface is in a constant waltz of environmental change, yet passive optical satellites are frequently blinded by monsoon storms, dense forest canopies, and darkness. To address the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Dancing with the SARs”, we developed EarthWaltz, an interactive, open-source global radar observatory that leverages active microwave Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the NASA-ISRO (NISAR) mission and partner constellations (ALOS-2, SAOCOM-1A, Sentinel-1, and RADARSAT-1).

EarthWaltz features a hardware-accelerated dual-map split curtain that allows users to peel back cloud-obscured optical satellite imagery and reveal calibrated 24 cm L-band and 9.3 cm S-band radar backscatter underneath. Users can explore six critical global biomes—from monsoon flood inundation across below-sea-level Kerala polders and hidden Amazon river surges to Himalayan glacial velocity, seismic fault slip in Turkey, and peatland wildfire risks in Sumatra. The platform integrates physical scattering telemetry, live NASA ASF/CMR STAC queries, and an innovative Web Audio sonification engine that translates radar backscatter rhythms into audible sound.

EarthWaltz is vital because it transforms abstract microwave physics into intuitive, multi-sensory insights, empowering disaster responders, resource managers, educators, and citizens with critical all-weather, day-or-night planetary situational awareness.
details:
EarthWaltz: Global SAR Observatory

Challenge: Dancing with the SARs (2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge)
Repository: https://github.com/Nekhal-james/EarthWaltz
Live Application: Built with Next.js 15, MapLibre GL JS, and Vercel Multi-Service Architecture EarthWaltz: Global SAR Observatory, https://earthwaltz.vercel.app

1. What does it do or how does it work?

The Core Concept

Optical satellites rely on sunlight and clear skies, meaning persistent monsoon storm clouds, dense tropical canopy, blizzard whiteouts, and nighttime conditions blind conventional cameras when critical disasters strike. EarthWaltz is an interactive, dual-mode web observatory that uses Active Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the joint NASA-ISRO SAR (NISAR) mission (dual-frequency 24 cm L-band and 9.3 cm S-band) alongside partner constellations (ALOS-2 PALSAR-2, SAOCOM-1A, Sentinel-1, and RADARSAT-1) to penetrate clouds and track planetary surface change in real time.

How It Works Under the Hood

  1. Hardware-Accelerated Dual-Map Split Curtain:
    • Two synchronized WebGL MapLibre GL JS map instances (radarMap and opticalMap) run concurrently with zero-latency bidirectional camera locking (jumpTo synchronized across pitch, bearing, zoom, and pan).
    • An interactive spatial curtain dynamically clips the top optical layer using GPU-accelerated CSS clipPath: inset(0 calc(100% - pos) 0 0) at 120 FPS.
    • Users can drag the curtain or click the Optical Split View toggle to directly compare what passive optical satellites see (often heavy cloud cover or smoke) against what active microwave radar reveals underneath.
    • HH Polarization (Water & Inundation): Identifies specular reflection on flat open water (σ0<−17.5 dB σ0 < -17.5 dB σ0<−17.5 dB, dark cobalt) versus corner-reflector "double-bounce" where standing water meets upright crops and building walls (σ0>−6.8 dB σ0 > -6.8 dB σ0>−6.8 dB, intense signal amber).
    • HV Polarization (Canopy & Biomass): Maps volume scattering across dense vegetation (σ0>−12.0 dB σ0 > -12.0 dB σ0>−12.0 dB, lush emerald) versus cross-polarized loss from clearcuts, logging roads, and fire scars (σ0<−17.5 dB σ0 < -17.5 dB σ0<−17.5 dB, vermilion).
    • InSAR Phase (Δϕ): Visualizes repeat-pass interferometric rainbow fringe cycles along active seismic fault lines, showing centimeter-scale surface deformation.
    • Coherence (γ): Highlights structural phase stability in urban areas (γ>0.72 > 0.72γ>0.72, crisp white) versus temporal decorrelation in turbulent water and windblown foliage (γ<0.30 < 0.30γ < 0.30, deep violet).
    • An in-browser algorithmic audio synthesizer built with the Web Audio API translates calibrated backscatter values and coherence stability into audible frequencies (60 Hz to 1.2 kHz60 Hz to 1.2 kHz60 Hz to 1.2 kHz), enabling users to literally hear the seasonal pulse and tidal rhythms of Earth's surface.
    • Direct integration with NASA Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) DAAC Vertex search and NASA Earthdata CMR STAC 1.0 APIs, backed by a microservice architecture for verified mission granules.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Unlocks Data Hidden from Optical Satellites: Proves the life-saving necessity of SAR by visually demonstrating how radar cuts through monsoon storm clouds, wildfire smoke, and darkness to reveal submerged communities and shifting ice.
  • Demystifies Complex Radar Physics: Traditional SAR data is locked behind specialized software (SNAP, ISCE3, Gamma) and raw polarimetric matrices. EarthWaltz translates complex decibels, wavelengths, and phase fringes into plain-English scattering mechanisms and intuitive visual heatmaps.
  • Multi-Sensory Accessibility: In addition to high-contrast cartographic visualizations, the built-in sonification engine provides an acoustic interface for blind, visually impaired, or auditory learners.
  • Zero-Install, High-Performance Web Access: Requires no specialized GIS software or plugins—anyone with a web browser on mobile or desktop can explore 30m global radar observations with sub-100ms response times.
  • Dual Exploration Modes: Features a guided Story Mode (overview narratives for the public and educators) and an analytical Instrument Workbench (with cursor telemetry HUD, swath opacity, multi-band toggles, and live STAC query tools for researchers).

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  1. Disaster Response & Humanitarian Relief:
    • Empowering civil defense teams during tropical monsoons (such as in Kerala, India) to identify submerged roads and isolated settlements beneath total cloud cover hours before floodwaters recede.
    • Giving environmental agencies and indigenous guardians near-real-time visibility into illicit deforestation frontiers and road networks hidden beneath the dense Amazon canopy.
    • Providing early-warning alerts for subterranean peatland moisture depletion in Sumatra to prevent catastrophic wildfires before ignition.
    • Tracking surface strain and fault slip across earthquake zones (e.g., the East Anatolian Fault in Turkey) and monitoring glacial retreat and moraine dam stability in the Himalayas to mitigate Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs).
    • Inspiring students, educators, and science communicators ahead of the official NISAR mission rollout by making active microwave remote sensing as engaging and accessible as browsing an online atlas.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

To develop EarthWaltz, we engineered a full-stack, hardware-accelerated web architecture using TypeScript, Next.js 15 (App Router), and React 19, structured into a Vercel Multi-Service Architecture with serverless Node.js API routes and an internal Python 3 microservice connected via runtime service bindings. The core mapping engine is powered by dual synchronized MapLibre GL JS and Deck.gl WebGL instances that deliver a seamless 120 FPS spatial split curtain via GPU-accelerated CSS clipping. Our user interface implements a Swiss Cartographic design system using Tailwind CSS, pairing Google Fonts’ Bricolage Grotesque with Atkinson Hyperlegible for high-contrast numeric readability, while the browser's native Web Audio API synthesizes live radar backscatter values into audible parametric frequencies.

For scientific data processing, our offline pipeline was built with Python 3, Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, and h5py to ingest and calibrate raw NISAR HDF5 data products (JPL D-102274 RevF) and compute physical backscatter anomalies against AWS Terrarium 30m Global DEM tiles and Esri World Imagery. The application interfaces directly with official Earth observation APIs—querying live SAR granule footprints via the NASA Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) DAAC Vertex API, searching STAC 1.0 catalogs through NASA Earthdata CMR, and overlaying true-color meteorological imagery from NASA EOSDIS GIBS WMTS—with end-to-end performance monitored using @vercel/analytics.

5. How is your project creative?

  • The "Earth’s Waltz" Metaphor: Rather than presenting SAR data as dry technical charts, we frame planetary surface change as an ongoing terrestrial choreography—the seasonal surge of floodwaters, the glacial crawl of mountain ice, the respiratory moisture cycle of agricultural soils, and the rhythmic fault slip of tectonic plates.
  • The Interactive Dual-Map Spatial Curtain: Instead of static before-and-after side-by-side screenshots, users actively drag a live curtain that peels back the cloud-covered optical satellite view to reveal the active microwave radar data beneath.
  • Algorithmic Radar Sonification: Converting decibel backscatter (σ0\sigma^0σ0) and phase stability into pitch, resonance, and harmonic rhythm allows users to experience satellite observations musically.
  • Selective Anomaly Overlay Design: Rather than draping an opaque, low-resolution raster across the entire screen, our pipeline selectively highlights physical anomalies (water double-bounce, deforestation scars, phase fringes) while allowing natural high-resolution terrain to show through underneath.
  • Swiss Cartographic Aesthetic: Designed with inspiration from Swiss topographic map standards—using Alabaster Vellum backgrounds (#F6F5F0), International Cobalt accents (#0047AB), disciplined survey rule lines, and accessible typography.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  1. Physical Accuracy & Scientific Provenance:
    • All microwave scattering thresholds were calibrated against empirical SAR literature: specular open water at < −17.5 dB < -17.5dB < −17.5 dB, double-bounce flooded vegetation at > −6.8dB > -6.8dB > −6.8dB, and volume scattering at > −12.0dB > -12.0dB > −12.0dB. Every study area links to real NASA DAAC granule IDs and WKT orbital swath footprints.
    • We selected 6 representative global study areas across 5 continents:
      • Kerala, India (Hometown Anchor): Monsoon flooding across Kuttanad's below-sea-level paddy polders.
      • Amazon Basin, Brazil: Hidden flood pulses and deforestation beneath the canopy.
      • Himalayas (Khumbu Glacier & Everest Massif): Glacial velocity and GLOF hazards.
      • Kahramanmaraş, Turkey: Coseismic fault rupture from the 2023 earthquakes.
      • Punjab, India: Agricultural soil moisture and intensive crop rotations through dust.
      • Sumatra, Indonesia: Subterranean tropical peatland moisture loss and fire warning.
    • Ensured the interface remains clean and uncluttered. The optical comparison split panel is off by default so users first see an unobstructed radar observatory, with on-demand controls to compare optical imagery and toggle cloud simulations.
    • Designed a multi-service Vercel architecture with decoupled Node.js and lightweight Python microservices (< 50 KB bundle), ensuring rapid global CDN delivery and smooth 60+ FPS map interaction.
    • Provided complete open-source transparency on GitHub under the MIT license, adhering to NASA Space Apps Challenge Super Intelligence (SI) attribution requirements with dedicated metadata tags and documentation.
